nameStory: The paper mulberry gets its name from its most famous use - making paper! For over 2,000 years, people in Asia have harvested the inner bark of this tree and processed it into fine paper and cloth. The scientific name 'papyrifera' literally means 'paper-bearing,' celebrating this tree's gift to human civilization.
description: Paper mulberry is a fast-growing deciduous tree that can reach 30-50 feet tall with a broad, spreading crown. Originally from East Asia, it's occasionally found in New England as an escaped ornamental. The tree has distinctively rough, heart-shaped leaves that can vary dramatically in shape - some are simple ovals while others are deeply lobed like mittens. Its gray-brown bark becomes deeply furrowed with age, and the tree produces separate male and female flowers on different plants.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with extremely variable shapes - some are simple ovals, others have 2-3 deep lobes like mittens. Feel rough and sandpapery on top, soft and fuzzy underneath. They're 3-8 inches long with prominent veins.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young bark is smooth and gray, becoming deeply furrowed and stringy with age. When scratched, reveals fibrous inner bark that's tough and papery - you can actually peel off strips.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Male and female flowers appear on separate trees in spring. Males form drooping, catkin-like clusters that are greenish-white. Females are small, round, and spiky, developing into orange-red aggregate fruits.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Fast-growing with a broad, irregular crown and often multiple trunks. Branches tend to be somewhat brittle and the tree has a somewhat unkempt, spreading appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Female trees produce small, round, orange-red fruits about 3/4 inch across with a bumpy, aggregate surface. They're sweet but somewhat dry when ripe in late summer.

habitat: In New England, paper mulberry is rarely found but may occur in disturbed urban areas, abandoned lots, and around old homesteads where it was planted as an ornamental. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade. Look for it in warmer, protected locations since it's not fully cold-hardy in northern New England.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge late in spring, and flowers appear in May before the leaves are fully developed. The distinctive sandpapery leaf texture is immediately apparent.
seasonality.summer: Full foliage shows the dramatic leaf shape variation. Female trees develop their characteristic orange-red fruits which ripen in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow before dropping relatively early. Ripe fruits may persist briefly on female trees.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the somewhat irregular growth pattern. The deeply furrowed bark and fibrous inner bark are most easily examined.

funFact: Paper mulberry bark is so incredibly strong that Pacific Island cultures have used it for centuries to make tapa cloth - fabric that's actually beaten out of tree bark! The fibers are so durable that ancient tapa cloth samples still exist in museums today, and the tradition continues in places like Fiji and Samoa.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with native red mulberry, but paper mulberry's leaves feel much more sandpapery and show more dramatic shape variation on the same tree. Paper mulberry's bark is also more stringy and fibrous when peeled, while red mulberry bark is smoother.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'mulberry,' this tree is only distantly related to our native red mulberry - they're in the same family but different genera. Paper mulberry is considered invasive in some warmer parts of the U.S., but cold winters generally keep it in check in New England.
compareHints: Paper mulberry is the only member of its genus in New England, so compare it with other mulberry family members like red mulberry and figs. Unlike red mulberry, paper mulberry has much rougher, more variable leaves and stringier bark. The leaf texture alone - feeling like fine sandpaper - immediately sets it apart from any native mulberry family member in our region.
